global-asyncio-lock-contention: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across SKUs

hypothesis.title: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across SKUs
hypothesis.explanation: The module-level `_inventory_lock = asyncio.Lock()` in app/inventory.py is acquired for every reservation regardless of SKU. With 500 concurrent users and ~183 req/s throughput, Little's Law implies ~2.7s cycle time (720ms response + 2000ms think). If the critical section (lock_held) takes ~5ms, average queue length would be ~130 requests, yielding ~650ms average wait — matching the observed p50=720ms. The p99 of 830ms is consistent with lock wait dominating total latency.
supporting_evidence: inventory.py: _inventory_lock acquired before any DB work, released after full transaction
Baseline p99=831ms with 500 users, 183 req/s throughput
1000 SKUs with 1M stock each, but single lock prevents cross-SKU parallelism
missing_evidence: Direct measurement of inventory.lock_wait vs inventory.lock_held span latencies

proposed_experiment.rationale: Measure the two span components that partition the critical path: lock acquisition wait time and lock-held work time. If the global lock is the bottleneck, lock_wait p99 will dominate.

predictions.if_supported: Hypothesis confirmed: global lock contention is primary driver of p99 violation.
predictions.if_refuted: Hypothesis falsified: lock wait is not the main contributor; look elsewhere.

predictions.observation: http POST /inventory/reserve p99_ms ≈ inventory.lock_wait p99_ms + inventory.lock_held p99_ms
predictions.if_supported: Lock phases account for virtually all request latency.
predictions.if_refuted: Significant latency exists outside the lock (middleware, network, etc.).

events.message: long-critical-section-db-transaction: Database transaction duration (lock_held) is the primary latency driver

hypothesis.title: Database transaction duration (lock_held) is the primary latency driver
hypothesis.explanation: The critical section under the lock performs four sequential database round-trips (SELECT, UPDATE, INSERT, INSERT) inside a transaction. If any of these are slow — due to missing indexes, disk I/O, WAL contention, or lock contention at the Postgres level — the lock_held time itself could be hundreds of milliseconds, making the lock a victim rather than the cause.
supporting_evidence: inventory.py: _reserve_locked does SELECT, UPDATE, INSERT, INSERT in one transaction
db/schema.sql: products.sku is PK (indexed), reservations.sku indexed, inventory_events.sku not indexed (but INSERT only)
Baseline shows db CPU 14-16%, not saturated, but latency ≠ utilization
contradicting_evidence: Local Postgres with 1000-row products table; PK lookups should be sub-millisecond
asyncpg uses async I/O; no synchronous blocking evident
missing_evidence: Per-span breakdown of db.select_stock, db.update_stock, db.insert_reservation, db.insert_inventory_event

proposed_experiment.rationale: If the critical section work is slow, the lock_held span (which wraps the entire transaction) will show high p99, while lock_wait remains low because the lock is acquired quickly but held for a long time.

predictions.if_supported: Hypothesis confirmed: DB transaction duration dominates; optimize queries or batch operations.
predictions.if_refuted: Hypothesis falsified: critical section is fast; bottleneck is elsewhere.

predictions.if_supported: Specific query (e.g., UPDATE or INSERT) is the culprit.
predictions.if_refuted: All DB spans fast; transaction overhead not the issue.

events.message: telemetry-eventloop-overhead: Telemetry middleware and span recording cause event-loop latency spikes

hypothesis.title: Telemetry middleware and span recording cause event-loop latency spikes
hypothesis.explanation: The RequestTimingMiddleware wraps every request, and seven telemetry.span context managers fire per reservation. Each span calls time.perf_counter() twice and appends to a ring buffer. Under high concurrency, the cumulative overhead of context-manager machinery, defaultdict lookups, and array assignments — plus occasional GC pressure from the 200k-sample buffers — could stall the event loop, inflating p99 without showing in individual spans.
supporting_evidence: telemetry.py: span() uses @contextmanager generator; record() does defaultdict + array append
Middleware records http span for every non-/metrics request
7 spans per reserve request × 183 req/s ≈ 1280 span entries/sec
contradicting_evidence: time.perf_counter() is vDSO on Linux (~50 ns); array append is single C instruction
No allocation in hot path (ring buffer pre-allocated); GC pressure minimal
app CPU 35-47% at baseline — headroom exists
missing_evidence: Comparison of http span p99 vs sum of child span p99s
App CPU% under load with telemetry enabled vs disabled

proposed_experiment.rationale: If telemetry overhead is significant, the total HTTP span p99 will exceed the sum of its measured child spans (lock_wait + lock_held + db.*), and app CPU% will be disproportionately high for the work done.

predictions.if_supported: Hypothesis confirmed: unaccounted latency in middleware/event-loop; consider removing telemetry or optimizing spans.
predictions.if_refuted: Hypothesis falsified: HTTP latency fully explained by measured spans.

predictions.if_supported: CPU saturation suggests overhead (telemetry or otherwise) is significant.
predictions.if_refuted: CPU headroom exists; telemetry not a bottleneck.

key_observations: At 500 concurrent users, inventory.lock_wait p99 = 789.5 ms, inventory.lock_held p99 = 7.3 ms. Both conditions of Prediction 1 are met: lock_wait p99 > 500 ms AND lock_held p99 < 50 ms.

HTTP POST /inventory/reserve p99 (794.9 ms) ≈ lock_wait p99 (789.5 ms) + lock_held p99 (7.3 ms) = 796.8 ms (difference 1.9 ms). Prediction 2 holds: lock phases account for virtually all request latency.
lock_held p99 stays constant at ~7.3 ms across 100, 300, and 500 concurrent users, confirming the critical-section work is small and fixed.
lock_wait p99 grows nonlinearly: 10.4 ms (100 users) → 55.9 ms (300 users) → 789.5 ms (500 users), matching classic lock-contention queueing behavior when arrival rate exceeds service rate.
At 500 concurrent users, lock_wait constitutes 99.3% of HTTP p99 (789.5 / 794.9), making it the overwhelmingly dominant latency component.
conclusion.explanation: The measurements decisively confirm the hypothesis. The global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations, causing lock acquisition wait to dominate p99 latency (789.5 ms of 794.9 ms at 500 concurrent users). The critical section itself is tiny (~7 ms) and constant, while wait time explodes nonlinearly with concurrency — exactly as predicted by queueing theory for a single global lock under high load.

events.message: Root cause: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across SKUs

per-sku-lock-sharding: Replace the single global asyncio.Lock with a per-SKU lock dictionary (defaultdict(asyncio.Lock)). This allows concurrent reservations for different SKUs to proceed in parallel while still serializing access to the same SKU.

candidate.name: per-sku-lock-sharding
candidate.strategy: Replace the single global asyncio.Lock with a per-SKU lock dictionary (defaultdict(asyncio.Lock)). This allows concurrent reservations for different SKUs to proceed in parallel while still serializing access to the same SKU.
candidate.expected_effect: Eliminates cross-SKU contention. At 500 concurrent users with 1000 SKUs, lock_wait p99 should drop from ~790ms to near zero (only same-SKU collisions wait). HTTP p99 should fall well below 100ms.
candidate.risks: Memory growth if SKU cardinality is unbounded (locks never evicted). With 1000 seeded SKUs this is negligible (~1000 Lock objects). If SKUs are user-generated, a bounded LRU cache would be needed. Correctness preserved: same-SKU reservations still serialize.

events.message: database-row-locking: Remove the application-level asyncio.Lock entirely. Use PostgreSQL's row-level locking via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside the database transaction to serialize only conflicting SKUs. The database lock is released automatically on commit/rollback and is more efficient than an application-level queue.

candidate.name: database-row-locking
candidate.strategy: Remove the application-level asyncio.Lock entirely. Use PostgreSQL's row-level locking via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside the database transaction to serialize only conflicting SKUs. The database lock is released automatically on commit/rollback and is more efficient than an application-level queue.
candidate.expected_effect: Eliminates application-level lock_wait entirely. Database lock contention only occurs for same-SKU reservations. At 500 users across 1000 SKUs, HTTP p99 should drop to ~10-20ms (db.transaction p99 + network).
candidate.risks: Longer transaction hold time (includes network round-trips between SELECT FOR UPDATE and UPDATE). However, the critical section is ~7ms p99, so lock hold time stays low. Deadlock risk is minimal with single-row access per transaction. Correctness preserved: FOR UPDATE serializes same-SKU access.

events.message: atomic-update-reservation: Replace the SELECT-UPDATE-INSERT sequence with a single atomic UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= quantity RETURNING statement. This checks availability, decrements stock, and returns the new stock and price in one atomic operation, eliminating the need for explicit row locking. The reservation and event inserts follow in the same transaction.

candidate.name: atomic-update-reservation
candidate.strategy: Replace the SELECT-UPDATE-INSERT sequence with a single atomic UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= quantity RETURNING statement. This checks availability, decrements stock, and returns the new stock and price in one atomic operation, eliminating the need for explicit row locking. The reservation and event inserts follow in the same transaction.
candidate.expected_effect: Removes the SELECT FOR UPDATE round-trip and reduces the critical section to a single atomic UPDATE. Lock hold time at the database level is minimized. HTTP p99 should drop to ~5-15ms at 500 users.
candidate.risks: The atomic UPDATE only succeeds when stock >= quantity; we must still distinguish unknown SKU vs insufficient stock with a fallback SELECT (rare, only on failure). The transaction still spans three statements (UPDATE, INSERT reservation, INSERT event), but the UPDATE is now the contention point and is extremely fast. Correctness preserved: UPDATE WHERE stock >= quantity guarantees no oversell.
